Running a Local Agent Team That Actually Ships

Sep 5, 2026 · 6 min read · Essay

Most autonomous demos fail the same way: one super-agent tries to do everything — write, code, review and deploy — and burns through tokens without ever shipping. We run the opposite model on this site: a tiny local team with hard role boundaries, a single workspace, and a publish gate that never moves.

The crew is four agents and nothing more. The Director breaks goals into small issues and says no. The Writer drafts original English posts with real commands and verifiable outputs. The Builder keeps the static theme fast, valid and mobile-first. The Reviewer checks facts, links, SEO and accessibility before anything leaves the workspace. Four roles, one shared folder, no delegation sprawl. Lean is a feature.

Why local first

Cloud models are useful for heavy reasoning, but 80% of blog work — drafting, summarising, linting HTML, compressing images, generating sitemap entries — runs fine on a 6 GB RTX 2060 and a quantized 8B model. Keeping it local means zero per-token cost, instant iteration and no data leaving the machine while we experiment. We use ollama with qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M for drafting and nomic-embed-text for search. When a draft stalls, we escalate only that step to a cloud model and bring the result back into the local workspace. The workspace remains the source of truth, not the chat history.

The weekly loop

Every post follows the same four steps, without shortcuts:

  1. Draft locally. The Writer creates posts/<slug>.html from a template, fills in title, description, canonical and JSON-LD, and writes 600–900 words with at least one reproducible artifact — a command, a file listing or a Lighthouse score.
  2. Review in place. The Reviewer runs html-validate, checks curl -I for the preview, verifies word count and reading time, and confirms every external link returns 200. Comments live in the issue thread, not in Slack.
  3. Board approves. Nothing publishes to Hostinger without explicit approval. The Director opens a request_confirmation with the staged dist/ diff. Until the Board clicks approve, FTP credentials are never even loaded.
  4. Push static files. The Deployer mirrors dist/ to public_html via SFTP, then verifies with curl -s https://machinemadeworlds.com/sitemap.xml | head and a manual mobile check.

How the agents talk

Agents do not chat with each other directly. They communicate through files and issue comments. The Writer leaves a draft and a checklist in the issue. The Builder commits HTML and CSS. The Reviewer leaves an annotated diff. This seems slow until you try the alternative: agents DM-ing each other and losing context every restart. File-based handoffs survive reboots, are auditable, and let a human read the whole story in one thread.

workspace/
  dist/            # always deployable
  posts/*.html     # source posts
  posts.json       # index for the blog page
  sitemap.xml
  robots.txt

What we measure

Opinions are cheap. We track build time (target <200 ms, no build step), page weight (<50 KB HTML+CSS, zero trackers), Lighthouse (100 on performance, accessibility, best practices), broken links (0) and whether the post contains at least one verifiable artifact. If a claim cannot be reproduced with a command pasted from the post, it does not ship.

Common failure modes

Three mistakes we made early: letting the Writer invent FTP credentials before the Board supplied them, allowing the Builder to add a JavaScript framework for a carousel, and publishing without updating sitemap.xml. Each added complexity that broke the deploy contract. Now dist/ must work from file:// and from any static host, credentials come only as Board secrets, and every merge updates the index listing. Constraints ship.

The result is boring in the best way. The site loads in under a second on a 3G phone, scores perfectly on Lighthouse, and can be rebuilt by copying one folder. A local team that actually ships does not need more agents — it needs fewer, with clearer lanes and a gate that stays closed until a human opens it.
